rationale: Asks for the shape of a histogram of an 'easy' test's scores, purely a distribution-shape question from Unit 1.
Bias identification and improved sampling design are Unit 1 sampling content, while the CI construction/interpretation and one-sample t-test for a mean are core Unit 4 inference skills.
Parts (a)-(b) are pure experimental-design/blocking content (Unit 1), while (c)-(d) require executing and interpreting a two-sample t-test (Unit 4).
Pure experimental-design item: treatment/control groups, outcome measurement, and random assignment are all Unit 1 design concepts.

Genuinely spans three units: the observational correlation (Unit 5), the causation-vs-correlation/confounding/experimental-design reasoning (Unit 1, the central theme), and the follow-up experiment's t-test conclusion with assumptions (Unit 4).
Simple computation of sample mean and standard deviation — core Unit 1 summary statistics.
Two-sample t-test for a difference in means: hypotheses, calculation, and conclusion are all Unit 4 content.
Entirely regression content: describing association, interpreting slope/intercept, assessing residual diagnostics, and recommending model use via R² — all Unit 5.
Generic confidence-interval-for-a-mean interpretation question; context ('population mean') places it in Unit 4 rather than Unit 3 (proportions).

Building the contingency table and computing conditional probabilities are Unit 2 (two categorical variables / conditional probability); the chi-square test of independence and its interpretation are Unit 3.
Segmented bar graph comparing the distribution of a categorical outcome (satisfaction) across two groups (before/after) — a two-categorical-variable comparison, Unit 2.

Comparing two students' relative standing on different tests via standardized (z-score) position is a Unit 1 'comparing distributions' skill; the CED does not give z-scores their own explicit topic in this list.
Curved residual pattern indicating a nonlinear relationship is core Unit 5 residual-diagnostics content.
Observational (self-reported, non-randomized) study and the causal-conclusion limits it implies is Unit 1 study-design content.
Standard deviation of a sum of independent random variables uses the Unit 2 rules for combining random variables (2.9).
Central Limit Theorem effect on shape and standard error of the sampling distribution of the sample mean as n increases — Unit 2 (2.12).
Checking np < 10 for the normal approximation to the sampling distribution of a sample proportion is the Unit 3 success/failure condition (3.2), which relies on the Unit 2 binomial background.
Correct interpretation of a confidence interval for a population proportion — Unit 3 (3.4).
Assessing whether conditions (small, strongly skewed sample) support a one-sample t-interval for a mean — Unit 4 (4.2).
Identifying a paired t-procedure (before/after on the same runners) as appropriate — Unit 4 mean-inference content (paired differences reduce to a one-sample test, 4.4/4.5).

Combining sparse categories so expected counts meet the chi-square minimum-count condition; this repo's Unit 3 topic list only names homogeneity/independence tests explicitly, though the item's scenario reads as goodness-of-fit, so the topic match is imperfect.

Interpreting a significant t-test for a regression slope, including the causation caveat for an observational study; inference for the slope is not a separately named Unit 5 topic in this list, so it is filed under the closest regression topics.
Simple z-score computation from a mean and SD — Unit 1 summary statistics.
Effect of changing one data value on the mean — Unit 1 summary statistics.
Identifying IQR as resistant to an outlier — Unit 1 summary statistics/spread.
Definition of the median for an even number of ordered observations — Unit 1 summary statistics.
Computing the IQR-based outlier fence — Unit 1 numerical/graphical summary content.
Relationship between mean and median for a roughly symmetric distribution with no outliers — Unit 1 distribution description.
Positive correlation between study hours and scores, with the correlation-does-not-prove-causation caveat — Unit 5 correlation content.
Computing a residual (observed minus predicted) — Unit 5 (5.4).
Appropriateness of prediction within the observed x-range (interpolation vs. extrapolation) — Unit 5 regression content.
Interpreting the slope of a least-squares regression line in context — Unit 5 (5.3).

Classic lurking-variable (ice cream/drownings) example framed around an observed correlation — primarily Unit 5 correlation content, with the confounding-variable concept also rooted in Unit 1 study design.
Effect of removing an influential point on the regression line and correlation — Unit 5.
Rationale for minimizing the sum of squared residuals in least-squares regression — Unit 5 (5.5).
Choosing a valid simple random sampling method from a numbered list — Unit 1 (1.11).
Rationale for stratified sampling over SRS — Unit 1 (1.11).
Identifying an observational study (no treatment assigned) — Unit 1 study design.
How blocking on age helps in a two-diet experiment — Unit 1 experimental design.
Identifying a plausible confounding variable (sleep and test scores) — Unit 1 confounding/design content.
What random assignment accomplishes (balancing lurking variables) — Unit 1 experimental design.
Undercoverage bias from a smartphone-only survey — Unit 1 (1.12 potential problems with sampling).
Purpose of double-blinding in an experiment — Unit 1 (1.13).
Recognizing a census (surveying every student) — Unit 1 sampling vocabulary.
Computing a conditional probability from a two-way table (athletes/honor roll) — Unit 2 (2.6).
Checking independence via P(A)P(B) = P(A and B) — Unit 2 (2.7).
Multiplication rule for a two-stage probability — Unit 2 conditional-probability content.
Computing the expected value of a simple discrete random variable — Unit 2 (2.8/2.9).
Complement rule for probability — Unit 2 (2.4).
Recognizing mutually exclusive events (heart and spade on one card) — Unit 2 (2.5).
Conditions for a binomial setting — Unit 2 (2.10).
Choosing combinations (unordered selection) is closest to the counting ideas underlying the binomial coefficient (Unit 2, 2.10), though combinatorics itself isn't a separately named topic here.
Addition rule, P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A and B) — Unit 2 (2.7).
Standard error of the sample mean (σ/√n) is introduced generically in Unit 2 (2.12); this item gives no inference (CI/test) context that would place it in Unit 4.
Mean of the sampling distribution of the sample mean equals the population mean — Unit 2 (2.12).
Central Limit Theorem explanation for approximate normality of the sampling distribution — Unit 2 (2.12).
Margin of error for a population-proportion confidence interval decreasing as n increases — Unit 3 (3.3).
Comparing standard error between two sample sizes from the same population — Unit 2 (2.12).
An estimator that consistently misses the true value even for large samples is describing bias — Unit 3 (3.1, estimators).
Standard error formula for a sample proportion — Unit 3 (3.2).
Whether a t-procedure is reasonable for a small, strongly skewed sample — Unit 4 (4.2 conditions).
Power = 1 - β is introduced generically as part of the Type I/II error framework — Unit 3 (3.8), though the concept applies to any inference procedure.
Correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval for a population mean — Unit 4 (4.3).
Constructing a (simplified) confidence interval for a population mean from x̄, s, n — Unit 4 (4.2).
Generic p-value decision with no proportion/mean context specified; filed under Unit 3 where p-values are first formally introduced (3.6/3.7).
Setting up H0/Ha for a one-proportion test — Unit 3 (3.5).
Grading judgment about the sign of a two-sample t-statistic under a two-sided alternative — Unit 4 two-sample mean inference.
Choosing a paired t-procedure over an independent two-sample test for matched before/after data — Unit 4 mean-inference content.

Reducing the standard error of a mean estimate by increasing sample size — the SE formula is introduced in Unit 2 (2.12); this generic item gives no explicit CI/test context that would place it in Unit 4.
Larger sample size increases the power of a test — Unit 3 (3.8, errors/power framework).
What a statistically significant two-sample t-test result does and doesn't establish — Unit 4.
Marginal probability/proportion from a two-way table — Unit 2 (2.1).
Bayes' theorem form for P(machine | defective) — Unit 2 conditional-probability content (2.6).
Choosing a chi-square test of independence for two categorical variables (snack preference by grade) — Unit 3 (3.14).
Computing an expected count for a chi-square table cell — Unit 3 (3.14).
Binomial probability P(X=0) for n=5, p=0.5 — Unit 2 (2.10).
Solving for the sample size needed to achieve a target standard error — Unit 2 (2.12) formula, generic (no CI/test framing).
Generic fail-to-reject decision from a p-value with no proportion/mean context — filed under Unit 3's p-value/decision topics (3.6/3.7).
Mean of a discrete random variable from its probability distribution — Unit 2 (2.8/2.9).
Interpolation (prediction within the observed x-range) vs. extrapolation — Unit 5.
Interpreting a regression slope in context — Unit 5 (5.3).
Interpreting R² as percent of variation explained by the linear model — Unit 5 (5.5).
Sign of a residual for a point above the regression line — Unit 5 (5.4).
Why a linear model is reasonable given a roughly linear scatterplot with no strong outliers — Unit 5.

Interpreting a confidence interval for a regression slope that excludes 0; inference for the slope is not separately named among this repo's Unit 5 topics, so it is filed under the closest regression topics.
Identifying an influential point in a scatterplot — Unit 5.
Choosing a two-sample t-procedure to compare means of two independent groups — Unit 4 (4.9).
Identifying a Type I error (rejecting a true null) — Unit 3 (3.8).
Rationale for a paired procedure when each subject is measured twice — Unit 4 mean-inference content.
Conclusion from a significant slope test plus the causation caveat — mainly Unit 5 regression inference, with the causal-inference limitation rooted in Unit 1 study design.
Comparing power across two studies differing in sample size and significance level — Unit 3 (3.8).

Why a 99% CI is wider than a 95% CI from the same sample (critical value effect); no proportion/mean context is given, so it is filed under Unit 3's first CI topic (3.3), though the concept applies equally to Unit 4 means.
Combines the logic of causal inference from a randomized experiment (Unit 1) with the two-sample t-test machinery used to detect the difference (Unit 4).
An entirely positive confidence interval for a slope implying evidence of a positive population slope — Unit 5 regression inference, not separately topic-listed.
Choosing a two-sample t-procedure when the response is quantitative and the predictor is a two-level categorical grouping — Unit 4.
Choosing a two-proportion z-procedure to compare two independent sample proportions — Unit 3.
Entirely about the sampling distribution of the sample mean: its mean, standard deviation, CLT-based normality, and how SD changes with n — all Unit 2 (2.12).
Classifying variables as categorical or quantitative is the Unit 1 topic 1.2 by definition.
Identifying population vs. sample is foundational Unit 1 sampling vocabulary.
Explaining why random sampling beats convenience sampling is core Unit 1 sampling-methods/bias content.
Explains the usefulness of the (approximately) normal sampling distribution via the CLT — Unit 2 content, though phrased loosely enough that it brushes against Unit 1 distribution description.
Distinguishing an experiment from a survey/observational study is Unit 1 study-design vocabulary.

Part (a) is basic variable classification (Unit 1, 1.2), but the bulk of the item — conditional distributions, a segmented bar graph, and comparing distributions across two categorical variables (transportation mode by distance group) — is Unit 2 (2.1/2.2), not Unit 1 as its stale internal topic tag suggests.
